tarjetas.p: A 7-year-old with an unrepaired complete cleft lip and palate; only one operation is possible. Lip or palate first?
tarjetas.r: Palate first. Its benefit (speech) is age-dependent; the lip's benefit (removing stigma) is not, so the lip can wait.

tarjetas.p: What is the general principle for choosing which cleft operation to do first in a late presenter?
tarjetas.r: Ask which benefit is time-dependent. Speech is learned in the first years, so the palate is the scarce window; lip stigma is removed equally at any age.

tarjetas.p: Does late cleft palate repair reliably improve speech?
tarjetas.r: No. It may not improve speech and may worsen speech predictability and nasal regurgitation (Schonmeyr 2015).

tarjetas.p: Standard age for primary cleft palate repair in high-resource settings vs reported average age of primary repair in sub-Saharan Africa
tarjetas.r: 9–12 months vs 10 years.

tarjetas.p: Approximate incidence of cleft lip and/or palate
tarjetas.r: 1 in 500–1000 births (Brazil: ~1:650–750, about 5000 new cases/year).

tarjetas.p: What percentage of all congenital anomalies occurs in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)?
Estimated global backlog of unrepaired clefts
tarjetas.r: 400 000 to 2 million patients.

tarjetas.p: Incidence vs burden: why do LMICs carry more of the cleft burden?
tarjetas.r: Not necessarily a higher rate per birth, but more births and fewer surgeons: more cases per surgical provider. It is a problem of access.

tarjetas.p: In Brazil, ~5000 clefts are expected per year but SUS registered <2000. Explanation and fix?
tarjetas.r: Underreporting (or overestimation of the expected rate). Fix: make cleft a compulsory notification. You can't plan what you don't measure.

tarjetas.p: What does the gap between these lines show, and which Lancet pillar does it belong to?
tarjetas.r: Expected (blue) vs SUS-reported (grey) cleft births: underreporting. Pillar: information management.

tarjetas.p: What is 'patient migration' in Brazilian cleft care?
tarjetas.r: Families travel from the North/North-East to a few centers: 4 centers in São Paulo do 67 % of the country's cleft care.

tarjetas.p: Patient migration: consequence for the family
tarjetas.r: Only the mother and child travel; the household breaks up and the cycle of poverty continues.

tarjetas.p: Patient migration: consequence for the child's treatment
tarjetas.r: They get the surgery but never the ancillary treatment or full rehabilitation (speech therapy, orthodontics, psychology), which must be near home.

tarjetas.p: Why are the dots on this map concentrated in the South-East, and what problem does it cause?
tarjetas.r: Primary repairs are done in a few accredited centers, so families from the North and North-East migrate and lose follow-up.

tarjetas.p: The key reframing of global cleft care: access to surgery or access to what?
tarjetas.r: Access to follow-up. The operation is once; follow-up lasts ~15 years and must be near home.

tarjetas.p: Three problems with surgical missions / operative camps (Patil 2011)
tarjetas.r: 1) Surgeons prefer lips over palates. 2) 86.4 % of camp patients weren't told about team care and follow-up (vs 100 % in centers). 3) No local infrastructure; they maintain dependence.

tarjetas.p: When are cleft missions appropriate, and when is supporting local centers better?
tarjetas.r: Missions: countries with little or no infrastructure (e.g., Haiti). Local centers: countries with growing infrastructure (Brazil, Chile, India): more efficient and sustainable.

tarjetas.p: Under what condition should a foreign cleft NGO be accepted?
tarjetas.r: If it trains and equips the local team (capacity building, e.g., Smile Train + SBCP 'Cleft Week') and doesn't neglect palates.

tarjetas.p: Minimum cleft team according to ACPA and Eurocleft
tarjetas.r: Plastic surgery, general dentistry, psychology, speech-language pathology and otolaryngology.

tarjetas.p: Who has the decisive role in patient adherence in Brazilian/Latin American cleft centers?
tarjetas.r: The social worker.

tarjetas.p: Minimum annual volume of new cases for a cleft center (Alonso)
tarjetas.r: 80–100 new cases per year.

tarjetas.p: Why not open a small cleft center in every town with a surgeon doing 10 cases/year?
tarjetas.r: Low volume and incomplete teams give worse results; gross sequelae need multiple costly reoperations at referral centers. 'Neither a non-prepared center nor a surgeon working alone should operate on a cleft patient.'

tarjetas.p: Decentralization vs fragmentation of cleft care
tarjetas.r: Decentralization: many complete centers (full team, ≥80–100 cases/year) close to families. Fragmentation: isolated low-volume surgeons.

tarjetas.p: Why did SUS hospitals run a monthly deficit treating clefts?
tarjetas.r: Flat monthly fee based on last year's production, with procedure prices below market: each extra patient is a cost.

tarjetas.p: Why does fee-for-service change a center's behavior compared with a flat fee?
tarjetas.r: Each operation brings income, so it incentivizes productivity. Risk: over-treatment, so add auditing (general knowledge).

tarjetas.p: Operation Smile Guwahati (Assam, India): the four partners and the results
tarjetas.r: Operation Smile (leadership, staff, supplies), National Rural Health Mission (fee-for-service, free for patients), Assam government (building), TATA (donations + auditing). After 5 years: 250–300 cases/month, self-sufficient, >90 % local staff.

tarjetas.p: Why must cleft care be free for the family, including follow-up and transport?
tarjetas.r: Out-of-pocket costs cause catastrophic / impoverishing expenditure; poor families drop out of follow-up.

tarjetas.p: The 5 pillars of a National Surgical Plan (Lancet Commission on Global Surgery)
tarjetas.r: Infrastructure, workforce, service delivery, financing, information management.

tarjetas.p: How is the Infrastructure pillar measured?
tarjetas.r: Proportion of the population with 2-hour access to a first-level surgical facility (also facility readiness and blood supply).

tarjetas.p: Classify by Lancet pillar: trained plastic surgeons leave cleft care for aesthetic surgery
tarjetas.r: Workforce (brain drain).

tarjetas.p: Classify by Lancet pillar: flat monthly fee causing hospital deficits
tarjetas.r: Financing.

tarjetas.p: Classify by Lancet pillar: centers opened without a full team or enough volume
tarjetas.r: Service delivery (quality and volume).

tarjetas.p: Lifetime economic benefit per cleft palate repair vs per cleft lip repair
tarjetas.r: Palate: $145 000–390 000. Lip: $52 000–141 000 (value of statistical life). The palate is worth more, consistent with repairing it first.

tarjetas.p: Cleft repair cost-effectiveness compared with other interventions
tarjetas.r: More cost-effective than treating some chronic diseases (heart disease, HIV) and than some vaccinations (BCG).

tarjetas.p: What does this image show and what does it tell you about cleft care in the region?
tarjetas.r: Adults with unrepaired clefts and no ancillary treatment: late presentation, common in underserved regions of Brazil.

tarjetas.p: Causes of brain drain among cleft surgeons in LMICs
tarjetas.r: Inadequate resources, lack of continuing education, professional isolation, and poor reimbursement (cleft is a low budget priority).
